name: Nahum
description: Threatened power · refuge · ruined defenses · cruelty · abandoned people

1.text: A revelation about Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.
The LORD is a jealous God and avenges. The LORD avenges and is full of wrath. The LORD takes vengeance on his adversaries, and he maintains wrath against his enemies.
The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. The LORD has his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
He rebukes the sea and makes it dry, and dries up all the rivers. Bashan and Carmel languish. The flower of Lebanon languishes.
The mountains quake before him, and the hills melt away. The earth trembles at his presence, yes, the world, and all who dwell in it.
Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the fierceness of his anger? His wrath is poured out like fire, and the rocks are broken apart by him.
The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and he knows those who take refuge in him.
But with an overflowing flood, he will make a full end of her place, and will pursue his enemies into darkness.
What do you plot against the LORD? He will make a full end. Affliction won’t rise up the second time.
For entangled like thorns, and drunken as with their drink, they are consumed utterly like dry stubble.
One has gone out of you who devises evil against the LORD, who counsels wickedness.
The LORD says: “Though they are in full strength and likewise many, even so they will be cut down and pass away. Though I have afflicted you, I will afflict you no more.
Now I will break his yoke from off you, and will burst your bonds apart.”

The LORD has commanded concerning you: “No more descendants will bear your name. Out of the house of your gods, I will cut off the engraved image and the molten image. I will make your grave, for you are vile.”

Behold, on the mountains the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace! Keep your feasts, Judah! Perform your vows, for the wicked one will no more pass through you. He is utterly cut off.

2.text: He who dashes in pieces has come up against you. Keep the fortress! Watch the way! Strengthen your waist! Fortify your power mightily!
For the LORD restores the excellency of Jacob as the excellency of Israel, for the destroyers have destroyed them and ruined their vine branches.
The shield of his mighty men is made red. The valiant men are in scarlet. The chariots flash with steel in the day of his preparation, and the pine spears are brandished.
The chariots rage in the streets. They rush back and forth in the wide ways. Their appearance is like torches. They run like the lightnings.
He summons his picked troops. They stumble on their way. They dash to its wall, and the protective shield is put in place.
The gates of the rivers are opened, and the palace is dissolved.
It is decreed: she is uncovered, she is carried away; and her servants moan as with the voice of doves, beating on their breasts.
But Nineveh has been from of old like a pool of water, yet they flee away. “Stop! Stop!” they cry, but no one looks back.
Take the plunder of silver. Take the plunder of gold, for there is no end of treasure, an abundance of every precious thing.
She is empty, void, and waste. The heart melts, the knees knock together, their bodies and faces have grown pale.
Where is the den of the lions, and the feeding place of the young lions, where the lion and the lioness walked with the lion’s cubs, and no one made them afraid?
The lion tore in pieces enough for his cubs, and strangled prey for his lionesses, and filled his caves with the kill and his dens with prey.

“Behold, I am against you,” says the LORD of Armies, “and I will burn her chariots in the smoke, and the sword will devour your young lions; and I will cut off your prey from the earth, and the voice of your messengers will no longer be heard.”

3.text: Woe to the bloody city! It is all full of lies and robbery—no end to the prey.
The noise of the whip, the noise of the rattling of wheels, prancing horses, and bounding chariots,
the horseman charging, and the flashing sword, the glittering spear, and a multitude of slain, and a great heap of corpses, and there is no end of the bodies. They stumble on their bodies
because of the multitude of the prostitution of the alluring prostitute, the mistress of witchcraft, who sells nations through her prostitution, and families through her witchcraft.
“Behold, I am against you,” says the LORD of Armies, “and I will lift your skirts over your face. I will show the nations your nakedness, and the kingdoms your shame.
I will throw abominable filth on you and make you vile, and will make you a spectacle.
It will happen that all those who look at you will flee from you, and say, ‘Nineveh is laid waste! Who will mourn for her?’ Where will I seek comforters for you?”
Are you better than No-Amon, who was situated among the rivers, who had the waters around her, whose rampart was the sea, and her wall was of the sea?
Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength. Put and Libya were her helpers.

Yet was she carried away. She went into captivity. Her young children also were dashed in pieces at the head of all the streets, and they cast lots for her honorable men, and all her great men were bound in chains.
You also will be drunken. You will be hidden. You also will seek a stronghold because of the enemy.
All your fortresses will be like fig trees with the first-ripe figs. If they are shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater.
Behold, your troops among you are women. The gates of your land are set wide open to your enemies. The fire has devoured your bars.
Draw water for the siege. Strengthen your fortresses. Go into the clay, and tread the mortar. Make the brick kiln strong.
There the fire will devour you. The sword will cut you off. It will devour you like the grasshopper. Multiply like grasshoppers. Multiply like the locust.
You have increased your merchants more than the stars of the skies. The grasshopper strips and flees away.

Your guards are like the locusts, and your officials like the swarms of locusts, which settle on the walls on a cold day, but when the sun appears, they flee away, and their place is not known where they are.
Your shepherds slumber, king of Assyria. Your nobles lie down. Your people are scattered on the mountains, and there is no one to gather them.
There is no healing your wound, for your injury is fatal. All who hear the report of you clap their hands over you, for who hasn’t felt your endless cruelty?

chapters.title: A breaking yoke changes who must fear
chapters.summary: This book is a message about Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. The LORD is slow to anger and great in power. He will not leave the guilty unpunished. Mountains quake before him, and no one can stand against his anger. He is good and a refuge in the day of trouble. He will make a full end of those who plot against him. He tells Judah he will break Assyria’s yoke. A messenger on the mountains brings news of peace.
chapters.meaning: The book of Jonah showed Nineveh spared. Nahum speaks in a later time about its fall. Verse 3 still calls the LORD slow to anger. It adds that he will not clear the guilty. Verses 7 and 8 set a refuge beside a flood. Verse 13 is spoken to Judah, which lived under Assyria’s demands (2 Kings 18:14). A broken yoke changes who has reason to fear.

lds.text: The lesson asks readers to consider power and mercy together in God’s character. How does the broken yoke explain Judah’s welcome for the message?

chapters.historicalNote: The opening describes God through storms, drying waters, and mountains that cannot stand. That immense power threatens enemies while offering refuge to people in trouble. The addressed voices then change between those facing destruction and those promised relief. Breaking a yoke describes release from another power's control, rather than escape from ordinary work. Judah can keep its feasts because the threatening intruder will no longer pass through. The same judgment therefore creates terror for one audience and welcome news for another.

chapters.title: The predator's den becomes a place of flight
chapters.summary: An attacker advances against Nineveh. Shields are red, and chariots flash like torches in the streets. The river gates are opened, and the palace collapses. The city is stripped, and its women moan like doves. People flee, and no one turns back. Plunderers carry off endless silver and gold. Nahum asks where the lions’ den is now. The lion once filled his caves with torn prey.
chapters.meaning: Verses 11–12 picture Nineveh as a den of lions. The lion killed enough for his cubs and his mates. He filled his caves with prey. So the city’s great wealth was plunder taken from others. Verse 9 shows that same treasure being carried off in turn. The question about the den is a taunt. Verse 13 says the voices of Assyria’s envoys will be heard no more.

lds.text: What does the lion’s stored prey suggest about the city’s wealth?

chapters.historicalNote: Commands to strengthen defenses begin a scene where those defenses cannot prevent the city's collapse. Flashing chariots, opened river gates, and a dissolving palace make power appear unstable. People flee despite shouted demands to stop, leaving treasure available for plunder. The poem then asks where the lions' secure feeding place has gone. A lion filling its den with prey gives an image for wealth gathered through violence. God's answer ends that predatory security by destroying chariots and silencing the city's messengers.

chapters.title: The ending explains why no one offers comfort
chapters.summary: Nahum cries woe to the city of blood, full of lies and plunder. Horsemen charge, and the dead lie in heaps. Nineveh sold nations by her charms and will be put to shame. No one will mourn her. She is no better than Thebes, the great city on the Nile. Thebes went into exile, and its infants were killed. Nineveh’s forts will fall like ripe figs. Her wound cannot be healed, and all who hear of it clap their hands.
chapters.meaning: Verse 7 asks who will mourn Nineveh or comfort her. Verse 19 gives the answer and the reason. Everyone who hears of her fall applauds. The verse ends with a question: who has not felt her endless cruelty? The applause is the verdict of her victims. Verses 8–10 recall the fall of Thebes as a warning. The book of Jonah also ends with a question about this city.

lds.text: Why does the final question connect the listeners’ applause with the city’s cruelty?

chapters.historicalNote: The bloody city's robbery gives the opening battle sounds and piled bodies a moral setting. Nineveh becomes a woman exposed and publicly shamed, joining military defeat with sexual humiliation. That violent image expresses the poem's attack on the city, not permission to assault women. The comparison with captured No-Amon challenges confidence in water defenses and powerful allies. Merchants and officials resemble disappearing insects, leaving scattered people without anyone to gather them. The final question explains the applause through cruelty experienced by those who hear the news.
